source: Some chapters back, one Bulkington was spoken of, a tall, newlanded mariner, encountered in New Bedford at the inn.

When on that shivering winter’s night, the Pequod thrust her vindictive bows into the cold malicious waves, who should I see standing at her helm but Bulkington! I looked with sympathetic awe and fearfulness upon the man, who in mid-winter just landed from a four years’ dangerous voyage, could so unrestingly push off again for still another tempestuous term. The land seemed scorching to his feet. Wonderfullest things are ever the unmentionable; deep memories yield no epitaphs; this six-inch chapter is the stoneless grave of Bulkington. Let me only say that it fared with him as with the storm-tossed ship, that miserably drives along the leeward land. The port would fain give succor; the port is pitiful; in the port is safety, comfort, hearthstone, supper, warm blankets, friends, all that’s kind to our mortalities. But in that gale, the port, the land, is that ship’s direst jeopardy; she must fly all hospitality; one touch of land, though it but graze the keel, would make her shudder through and through. With all her might she crowds all sail off shore; in so doing, fights ’gainst the very winds that fain would blow her homeward; seeks all the lashed sea’s landlessness again; for refuge’s sake forlornly rushing into peril; her only friend her bitterest foe!

Know ye now, Bulkington? Glimpses do ye seem to see of that mortally intolerable truth; that all deep, earnest thinking is but the intrepid effort of the soul to keep the open independence of her sea; while the wildest winds of heaven and earth conspire to cast her on the treacherous, slavish shore?

But as in landlessness alone resides highest truth, shoreless, indefinite as God—so, better is it to perish in that howling infinite, than be ingloriously dashed upon the lee, even if that were safety! For worm-like, then, oh! who would craven crawl to land! Terrors of the terrible! is all this agony so vain? Take heart, take heart, O Bulkington! Bear thee grimly, demigod! Up from the spray of thy ocean-perishing—straight up, leaps thy apotheosis!

modern_en.title: Chapter 23 — The Lee Shore
paragraphs: Some chapters back, a man named Bulkington was mentioned — a tall, recently landed sailor encountered at the inn in New Bedford.

When, on that shivering winter's night, the Pequod thrust her vengeful bows into the cold, malicious waves, who should I see standing at her helm but Bulkington! I looked at the man with sympathetic awe and dread. Here was someone who, in midwinter, having just landed from a dangerous four-year voyage, could so restlessly push off again for yet another stormy term at sea. The land seemed to scorch his feet. The most wondrous things are always the ones that cannot be spoken; deep memories yield no epitaphs; this six-inch chapter is the stoneless grave of Bulkington. Let me say only that it went with him as with the storm-tossed ship that drives miserably along a lee shore. The port would gladly give shelter; the port is compassionate; in the port there is safety, comfort, a hearth, supper, warm blankets, friends — everything that is kind to our mortal selves. But in that gale, the port, the land, is that ship's direst danger. She must flee all hospitality. One touch of land, even if it only grazed the keel, would make her shudder through and through. With all her might she crowds on every sail to get offshore, and in doing so fights the very winds that would gladly blow her homeward. She seeks the lashed sea's landlessness again, rushing forlornly into danger for the sake of refuge — her only friend her bitterest enemy!

Do you understand now, Bulkington? Do you seem to catch glimpses of that mortally unbearable truth — that all deep, earnest thinking is nothing but the brave effort of the soul to keep the open independence of her sea, while the wildest winds of heaven and earth conspire to cast her on the treacherous, enslaving shore?

But since the highest truth lives only in landlessness — shoreless and boundless as God — it is better to perish in that howling infinity than to be ingloriously dashed against the lee shore, even if that shore meant safety! For who, worm-like, would crawl like a coward to land! Terrors of the terrible! Is all this agony in vain? Take heart, take heart, O Bulkington! Bear up grimly, demigod! Up from the spray of your ocean death — straight up — leaps your apotheosis!

modern_da.title: Kapitel 23 — Læsiden
paragraphs: For nogle kapitler siden blev en mand ved navn Bulkington nævnt — en høj, nyligt landsat sømand, man mødte på kroen i New Bedford.

Da Pequod den kolde vinternat, hvor alt rystede, stak sin hævngerrige stævn ind i de kolde, ondskabsfulde bølger, hvem skulle jeg så se stå ved roret andre end Bulkington! Jeg så på manden med medfølende ærefrygt og gru. Her var en, som midt om vinteren, lige hjemvendt fra en farlig fireårig rejse, kunne drage ud igen så rastløst, til endnu en stormfuld tid på havet. Landet syntes at svide under hans fødder. Det mest vidunderlige er altid det, der ikke kan siges; dybe minder giver ingen gravskrifter; dette kapitel på seks tommer er Bulkingtons gravsted uden sten. Lad mig kun sige, at det gik ham, som det går et stormslået skib, der elendigt driver ind mod en læ kyst. Havnen ville gerne give ly; havnen er medfølende; i havnen er der tryghed, bekvemmelighed, et ildsted, aftensmad, varme tæpper, venner — alt, hvad der er rart for vores dødelige selv. Men i den storm er havnen, landet, skibets værste fare. Det må flygte fra al gæstfrihed. Én berøring af land, selv hvis den bare strejfede kølen, ville få det til at ryste helt igennem. Af alle kræfter sætter det alle sejl for at komme fri af kysten, og derved kæmper det mod netop de vinde, der gerne ville blæse det hjem. Det søger igen det piskede havs landløshed og styrter fortabt ud i fare for at nå ly — dets eneste ven er dets bitreste fjende!

Forstår du det nu, Bulkington? Kan du ane noget af den dødeligt uudholdelige sandhed — at al dyb, alvorlig tænkning kun er sjælens tapre bestræbelse på at bevare sit åbne havs uafhængighed, mens himlens og jordens vildeste vinde sammensværger sig om at kaste hende op på den forræderiske, slavebindende kyst?

Men da den højeste sandhed kun bor i landløsheden — kystløs og grænseløs som Gud — er det bedre at gå under i den hylende uendelighed end at blive smadret uhæderligt mod den læ kyst, selv om den kyst betød redning! For hvem ville som en orm kravle som en kujon i land! Rædsler over rædsler! Er al denne smerte forgæves? Tag mod til dig, tag mod til dig, o Bulkington! Hold stand med sammenbidte tænder, halvgud! Op fra sprøjtet af din død i havet — lige op — springer din ophøjelse til guddom!
